messages.author: 9c320f4f05eeb4ee
messages.subject: Simple bivariate mixture model
parts:
Hi all,

I'm just about to teach mixture models and would like to get the students excited about STAN, which is definitely an awesome tool.

Inspired by other examples, I wrote this simple mixture model below.

data {
  int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components
  int<lower=1> N; // number of data points
  vector[2] y[N]; // observations
}

parameters {
  simplex[K] theta;        // mixing proportions
  vector[2] mu[K];         // locations of mixture components
  cov_matrix[2] sigma[K];  // covariance matrices of mixture components
}

model {
  real ps[K];
  for (k in 1:K)
    mu[k] ~ normal(0, 10);

 for (n in 1:N) {
        for (k in 1:K) {
          ps[k] <- log(theta[k])
                   + multi_normal_log(y[n],mu[k],sigma[k]);
      }
        increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
      }
}


With very simple data (e.g. mu=[[4,4], [1,1]], sigma=[[[1, 0],[0, 1]], [[1,0],[0,1]]], theta=[0.7, 0.3]), it seems not to work well at all. In fact, it keeps getting "LDLT_Factor of covariance parameter is not positive definite.", i.e. nan conditional variances (should I do something on the prior for sigma? What? I tried several things...). What am I doing wrong?

If this was responded earlier, I apologize and thank whoever can redirect me to the right link.

Thanks!
  Francisco

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Simple bivariate mixture model
parts: Hi, yes, I think you’ll need some prior for sigma.  Also you need to identify the mixture components, otherwise you have aliasing.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Simple bivariate mixture model
parts:
In particular, see the regression chapter of the manual for suggestions
on covariance matrix priors. Without a prior, you're likely running into
problems with variance components approaching zero and resulting in poorly
conditioned matrixes for solving (as required in the multivariate normal density).
At least that's what happens in the univariate case.

- Bob
